A burglar who stole thousands of dollars' worth of Pokemon trading cards from a local business has been given "an opportunity to reinvent" himself.

Login or signup to continue reading

Jack Carbone, aged in his mid-30s, committed a string of burglaries over several months, including breaking into multiple businesses to steal alcohol and cigarettes.

He was handed a sentence of more than four years and two months in the ACT Supreme Court on Monday, November 16. The custodial part of the sentence was suspended for him to enter into a drug and alcohol treatment order.

Carbone was required to admit himself into a residential rehabilitation program that afternoon.

He previously pleaded guilty to three counts of aggravated burglary by joint commission, and single counts of burglary and contravening a court order.

In February 2026, about 2am, Carbone broke into the Collectors Colosseum in Acton using his body to force through the door. He stole several display cases with the valuable cards inside and tried to ride off with them on an e-bike.

He didn't get far before he forced the cases open, placed the trading cards into a duffle bag and rode off again.

On March 6, police searched Carbone's home in Belconnen, where he was living in breach of his bail conditions, and found three of the cards.

More cards were found during a search of another address. One of the recovered cards was worth $2000, another $550.

A number of cards stolen from the store were not recovered. Police have urged anyone with information about the sale of Pokemon trading cards in Canberra to come forward.

On Monday, Justice Verity McWilliam said the stolen cards were collectors' items and "difficult, if not impossible, to replace".

She said the owner of the business was "emotionally and financially invested" in the store and had suffered financial stress as a result of the theft.

"The burglary has been traumatic for him," Justice McWilliam said.

The judge found that Carbone had been exposed to childhood trauma and had a severe substance abuse disorder at the time of his crimes.

He also had "little to no current ability" to pay a fine or reparations to the owner.
